bib.title: Chapter 10. Testing: Evaluation, Monitoring, and Continuous Improvement (Learning LangChain)

question: How should an LLM application be tested, evaluated, monitored and improved across design, preproduction and production stages, using LangGraph and LangSmith?
contributions: A three-stage testing cycle (design, preproduction, production)
Preproduction datasets, evaluator types, regression testing and three-level agent testing
Production tracing, online evaluation and feedback

results.claim: A small evaluation dataset is 10 to 50 quality manually curated examples, extended later with production edge cases.
results.setup: Manually curated examples for a LangSmith dataset; no empirical basis given
results.quote:
A small dataset consists of between 10
and 50 quality examples.

results.claim: Agent runs in the book's examples are repeated three times because outcomes vary run to run.
results.setup: SQL agent examples with langsmith evaluate()

results.claim: Start evaluation with heuristic evaluators, then human evaluators, then LLM-as-a-judge to automate human review.
results.quote:
To get started with evaluation, start simple with heuristic evaluators.
Then implement human evaluators before moving on to LLM-as-a-judge
to automate your human review.

results.claim: Judge prompts should be simple and replicable; avoid 0 to 10 scores with vague distinctions.
results.quote:
avoid asking an LLM
to produce scores on a range of 0 to 10 with vague distinctions between scores.

results.claim: Human corrections to judge outputs are stored as few-shot examples and fed into later judge prompts.
results.quote:
human corrections to LLM-as-
a-judge outputs are stored as few-shot examples, which are then fed back
into the prompt in future iterations.

results.claim: Agents should be tested at three granularities: response, single step, trajectory.
results.setup: Agent evaluation, SQL agent example (5 question-answer pairs)
results.quote: Ideally, agents should be tested at three different levels of granularity:

results.claim: Online evaluation is reference-free and real time, because production has no grounded reference responses.
results.quote:
This reference-free, real-time evaluation is
often referred to as online evaluation.

results.claim: User feedback can be attached to any trace or span in LangSmith.
results.setup: LangSmith tracing, explicit or implicit feedback
results.quote:
you can at‐
tach user feedback to any trace or intermediate run (that is, span)

results.claim: Production errors should be added to the test dataset; phased beta release helps build a ground-truth dataset.
results.quote:
You can add these errors into your test dataset for
offline evaluation in order to prevent recurrences of the same issues.

results.claim: AI test suites may not reach a perfect score, so results must be tracked over time against a baseline.
results.quote:
testing AI ap‐
plications may not always lead to a perfect score on the evaluation
dataset.

limits: No experiments or measured results; all content is workflow guidance tied to LangSmith and LangGraph.
The 10 to 50 example size is asserted without evidence.
Code is dated (hub.pull, get_relevant_documents, langchain_core.pydantic_v1); the JavaScript in_order check only tests presence, not order, unlike the Python subsequence check.
Sample SQL agent dataset has only 5 examples; no judge agreement or cost figures given.
practices: Test at three stages: design (runtime assertions fed back to the LLM), preproduction (regressions before release), production (monitoring feeding back to design). Where: Testing Techniques.
Use an LLM to grade retrieval relevance and fall back to web search in self-corrective RAG. Where: Design Stage.
Build datasets from manually curated examples, application logs and synthetic data. Where: Creating Datasets.
Choose LangSmith dataset type kv, llm or chat; kv is the default and most flexible. Where: Creating Datasets.
Start with heuristic evaluators, then human, then LLM-as-a-judge. Where: Defining Your Evaluation Criteria.
Use few-shot human corrections to align the LLM judge. Where: Improving LLM-as-a-judge.
Use pairwise evaluation when ranking outputs is easier than scoring. Where: Pairwise evaluation.
Set a baseline run and compare experiments to detect regressions. Where: Regression Testing.
Test agent final response with an LLM judge, a single step with a binary tool-selection score, and trajectory with any-order, in-order and exact-match checks. Where: Agent testing.
Enable tracing with environment variables and review trace volume, error rate, latency, token count and cost. Where: Tracing.
Collect user feedback and judge feedback online; use LLM-as-a-judge for tagging when no labels exist. Where: Production.
Release in phases to beta users to build a ground-truth dataset. Where: Monitoring and Fixing Errors.
